Parent's note, the night before Harish leaves for Pune
Two weeks ago Harish sat at the dining table with a sheet of paper and made six headings: documents, admission, bank, medicines, clothes, contacts. I sat with him and we filled each one together.
Every evening since, we have ticked a few things off. Day two: photocopies of marksheets and ID, in a plastic folder. Day four: the admission letter and fee receipt, printed twice. Day six: his debit card activated and the bank app set up, with me checking. Day nine: his allergy tablets from the doctor, with the prescription. Day eleven: his cousin Anand's number in Pune, the hostel warden's, and ours, written on a card as well as saved.
He insisted the essentials go in last. “If they're under the T-shirts, I'll never find them at the station.” Tonight the clothes went in first, and the folder, tablets and card went in last, on top, in the small bag he will carry.

qa.a: His allergy tablets from the doctor, with the prescription.

qa.q: What does Harish's insistence on packing the essentials last suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt careful and a bit anxious about the important papers, wanting them on top and easy to reach at the station.

qa.q: What else could Harish add to the checklist before leaving?
qa.a: Photos of key documents kept safely, and the route from the station to the hostel, so a lost folder or late train is less of a crisis.

qa.q: How might Anand see the preparation?
qa.a: Anand, the cousin in Pune, would likely be reassured that Harish arrives organised, with contacts written down.

grounding: A parent notes a teen listing documents, admission papers, bank access, medicines, clothes and contacts, ticking them off over two weeks, and packing the essentials last.

Uma had nine days before classes began in Bengaluru and one weekend when both parents could travel with her. The coaching institute's hostel had a waiting list, and the paying-guest places nearby all promised “safe, homely food, walking distance”.
So on the train they made a table: hostel or PG, rent, meals, curfew, distance, what reviews said. Two PGs had reviews mentioning broken locks, so they crossed those off. Then Uma called Hrithik, a senior from her school who had studied there last year.
“Ask about the walk at night,” he said. “The lane behind Green Villa has no lights. And the food at Sai PG is fine; the other one skipped dinner twice a week.”
On Saturday, in heavy rain, they visited three places. At Sai PG, Uma checked the lock on the door and the lights on the lane, and asked two girls on the stairs what the warden was like. Only after that did Appa pay the deposit.

qa.a: It has no lights.

qa.a: Uma was probably anxious about the short deadline but determined to see the places herself before any deposit was paid.

qa.a: Talk to the warden directly about rules and emergencies, and walk the route to the institute at the hour Uma would use it.

qa.a: Hrithik probably feels useful and trusted, glad to pass on details a review wouldn't show.

In the crowded lanes near the coaching centres of Mukherjee Nagar in Delhi, Omkar and his father spent Sunday doing what they had planned on paper. The list in Omkar's notebook had four places: the institute hostel and three paying-guest houses, with columns for rent, food, distance and “what seniors say”.
The night before, Omkar had messaged Zubin, a senior from their town, now in his second year. Zubin was blunt. “The cheap PG near the market floods every August. The hostel food is boring but regular. Check whether the PG gate closes at night.”
So they checked. At the first PG the owner said “all safe, no problem”, but the fire exit was padlocked. They left. At the second, the commute was forty minutes by bus, not the “ten minutes” in the advert. At the hostel, Omkar tasted the dal, saw the warden's desk by the gate, and walked the route to class himself.
They paid the hostel deposit only on the way out.

qa.a: The fire exit was padlocked.

Before the move, a Sunday in May: Avni sits at the dining table with her parents and makes two lists. Fixed: hostel rent, the mess, the monthly bus pass. Changing: books and printouts, phone recharge, snacks, the odd auto ride. “What if something breaks?” she thinks aloud. “A phone, my specs, a sudden trip home.” So she adds a small reserve line at the bottom that she won't touch for ordinary things. Together they agree one monthly amount that covers all of it.
Week three in Chennai: Avni's specs snap in the lab. Her roommate Maria watches her open the notebook, check the reserve line, and pay the optician without calling home in a panic.
End of the first term: She compares the notebook with the plan. Snacks went over; printouts came in under. She tells her parents on the weekly call, and together they adjust next term's split.

qa.a: Avni was worried about sudden costs like a broken phone or a trip home, and wanted to feel secure without a panicked call.

qa.a: Looking at the notebook every few weeks, not only at term end, and talking to her parents early if one line keeps running over.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study

passage:
Trisha, you're asking how much to ask your parents for each month. Let me tell you how I did it when I went to Madurai for my pre-university course.
Your great-grandfather sent me a money order on the first of every month. The first month I spent freely in the first week, and by the twentieth I was eating only rice and pickle and borrowing bus fare. I felt so ashamed.
So in the second month I sat down with a notebook. Fixed things first: hostel fees, the mess, the bus. Then changing things: books, soap, the cinema once a month. And at the bottom, a separate line: a small amount in a tin under my bed, only for emergencies. My roommate used to tease me, “Rukmini and her tin.” Then I wrote to my father, and we agreed on one amount that covered it all.
In the fourth month I had a high fever one night. The tin paid the auto to the clinic. I didn't have to send a frightened telegram home.
So, Trisha: list first, then ask.

qa.q: What paid for the auto to the clinic?
qa.a: The tin under the bed.

qa.q: How did young Rukmini feel by the twentieth of the first month?
qa.a: Rukmini felt ashamed, eating only rice and pickle and borrowing bus fare.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things for Rukmini?
qa.a: Sitting down in the second month to list fixed and changing costs, keep an emergency tin, and agree one amount with her father.

qa.q: How might Rukmini's father have felt about the letter agreeing a monthly amount?
qa.a: The father was probably relieved and proud, seeing a clear plan instead of worried letters asking for more.

grounding: An elder recalls listing fixed and changing costs, keeping a small emergency reserve, and agreeing a monthly amount with her father so a sudden fever didn't become a crisis.

In my first week at the hostel in Pune, I made myself a rule: one new connection a day. I'm Rukmini, and I'd heard enough stories about people who stay in their rooms and cry till Diwali.
Day one, I knocked on the doors on either side and said hello; one neighbour lent me a bucket. Day two, I saved the warden's number and my local guardian's, Kavita Aunty in Kothrud, and stuck them on my cupboard. Day three, Sumit from my maths class said a few of them solved problems together in the library after dinner. I went, was useless, and they asked me back anyway.
I also fixed my calls home: Tuesday and Saturday, eight o'clock, half an hour. When I felt homesick in between, I wrote it in my diary instead of calling.

The night before leaving her town, Barabanki, for college in Lucknow, Zeenat couldn't sleep, so she ran the first week in her head like a film.
Monday morning. Alarm at six-thirty. What if the hostel bathroom queue is long? Then shower at night. She wrote that down.
Getting to college. The bus from the hostel gate, number 27. What if she misses it? She opened the map on her phone and saved the route, then wrote the walking directions on paper too, in case the phone died.
Lunch. Where? Sudha, her cousin who had studied there, had said the canteen near the library was cheap. Zeenat put some cash in her pencil box, separately, for days the card machine didn't work.
What if she got lost? Ask a guard or a shopkeeper, not a stranger in a car.
By midnight her list had eleven small answers. The knot in her stomach had loosened. She slept.

qa.q: Which bus goes from the hostel gate?
qa.a: Number 27.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel after writing the eleven answers?
qa.a: Zeenat felt calmer, the knot in her stomach loosening enough to sleep.

qa.q: What else could Zeenat plan for the first week?
qa.a: Where to go if she feels unwell or lost, like the warden's office and a trusted adult's number, so bigger worries also have answers.

Thursday, week 3
I thought by now I'd have a gang. That's what everyone said: you'll make friends in the first week. The first week I was busy. The second week I kept waiting. Now it's the third week, and I eat dinner alone at the corner table in the mess, and Ganga from the next room is nice but has friends from school already.
I lay on my bed at seven today and felt like the walls were closing in. My chest was tight. I looked up train times home. I actually filled in half the withdrawal form on the college site.
Everyone else seems settled. Maybe I'm just not a hostel person. Maybe I made the wrong choice.
Called Ammi. Told her I want to come home. She said, “Noor beta, three weeks is nothing. Don't fill any form. Come home for the weekend and we'll talk properly.”
I don't know. It feels like it'll always be like this.

qa.q: What did Noor fill in half of?
qa.a: Half the withdrawal form on the college site.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling on the bed at seven?
qa.a: Noor felt panicky and trapped, chest tight, as if the walls were closing in.

qa.q: What would help Noor more than leaving after three weeks?
qa.a: Knowing that settling in usually takes months, and taking small steps like joining a club or talking to the warden while giving it time.

qa.q: How might Ammi see Noor's call?
qa.a: Ammi is probably worried but steady, wanting Noor to slow down, come home for the weekend and talk before deciding anything.

In her first month, Ira from Room 9 skipped breakfast almost every day. She would sleep past seven and run for the bus with nothing, and her class teacher told me she was drifting off in the late-morning lectures. She also tried to study in the evenings, when the common room is at its loudest.
In the third week she came to me herself and said, “Something isn't working.” We talked it through. Since then she has changed three things. She sleeps and wakes at fixed times: lights off at eleven, up at six-fifteen. She has signed up with the tiffin service run by Ujjwal's family two lanes away, and collects breakfast on her way to the bus. And she studies from five to seven in the morning and after nine at night, when the hostel is quiet.
Her teacher says she is much more alert. She looks happier at the gate, too.

qa.a: Ira was probably frustrated and tired, but ready to change rather than keep struggling.

qa.q: What else could Ira do if the new routine slips?
qa.a: Check in with the warden again and adjust one thing at a time, such as the study slot, rather than dropping the whole routine.

qa.a: They gain a regular customer and probably feel good that their breakfast helps a student far from home.

I'm Sarita, and my room is across the corridor from Bhupen's in our college hostel. For his first two months, his light was on at two and three in the morning. He stopped coming to the mess on weekends. When I asked how he was, he always said, “Fine, just tired.”
In the ninth week I saw him knock on the warden's door after dinner and go in for a long time. The next Tuesday he was in the counsellor's waiting room when I went in for my scholarship form.
Things changed slowly after that. On Saturday mornings he started leaving early with the photography club, camera round his neck. His light went off earlier. He told me once that he'd booked a train home for the Diwali break and was counting the weeks, but in a good way.
I don't know what he said to the warden. But I think asking was the hard part.

qa.q: How does the change look to Sarita?
